name: Gunpowder foundation
note: ROME ALREADY HAS THIS. Saltpetre, charcoal, sulfur mixed in open vessels. Unreliable, separates in transport, cannot sustain rapid fire.

name: Serpentine powder
note: Incorporates ingredients into granules by pounding with water, forming a paste that dries into grains. Granules separate less during transport and handling than loose powder.

name: Corned gunpowder
note: Corning is what makes gunpowder work at all. Smaller, denser granules with better ingredient distribution burn faster and generate higher pressure. The critical step between unreliable and practical.

name: Powder mill
note: Water-powered pounding mills for consistent granule production at scale. First application of water power to military supply.

name: Incorporating mill
note: Water-powered wet incorporation of ingredients at scale. High explosion risk during operation and storage, hence remote location requirement and danger premiums for workers.

name: Slow match
note: Saltpetre-soaked cord burns at a steady rate, allowing a musketeer to ignite the touchhole without a spark steel. The slow match tether extends to modern range.

name: Quick match
note: Sulfur accelerates burn rate reliably. Enables faster priming sequences and synchronized multi-gun barrages in artillery.

name: Wheel lock mechanism
note: Spring-driven spinning wheel strikes flint or pyrite against steel frizzen to generate sparks. Eliminates need for slow match and frees hands, but mechanism is complex and expensive.

name: Matchlock mechanism
note: Serpentine arm holds lit slow match and pivots into touchhole by trigger lever. Simpler and cheaper than wheel lock, becomes dominant for musketeers because ammunition availability matters more than convenience.

name: Flintlock mechanism
note: Flint held in cock strikes steel frizzen, sparks fall into priming pan. More reliable than wheel lock, simpler than both, dominant by 1700. Enables fast aimed fire.

name: Percussion cap
note: Mercury fulminate in small copper cup detonates reliably when struck by hammer. Replaces flint-spark with chemical ignition, enabling breech-loading and faster fire.

name: Paper cartridge
note: Powder and ball wrapped in paper tube, carried at the hip. Quadruples loading speed compared to separate powder horn and pouch. Transformation of fire rate through ammunition packaging.

name: Metallic cartridge
note: Brass case contains powder, primer, and bullet in one unit. Self-contained; does not leak or absorb moisture. Requires precision manufacture but enables reliable rapid fire.

name: Centrefire primer
note: Percussion compound in center of cartridge base, struck by firing pin rather than edge. Enables breech block design and rapid mechanical operation.

name: Rifling
note: Helical grooves in barrel impart spin to projectile, stabilizing flight and improving accuracy beyond 100 yards. Cost in barrel wear and loading complexity offset by lethal accuracy at range.

name: Minie ball
note: Conical lead projectile with hollow base. Skirt expands under powder gas to grip rifling, then sheds when leaving barrel. Combines ease of loading with stability from rifling.

name: Breech-loading rifle
note: Loading from the rear of the barrel eliminates need for ramming. Soldier can load from prone position or behind cover. Triples sustained fire rate and changes infantry tactics from advance to entrenchment.

name: Bolt-action rifle
note: Rotating bolt with cam-operated locking, opened and closed by hand lever. Repeats rapidly and runs within tolerances. Becomes the dominant rifle design because it is simple, robust, and fast.

name: Magazine
note: Spring-loaded box stores cartridges and feeds them upward to chamber. Enables rapid fire without manual feeding. Magazine design determines whether rates of fire double or triple.

name: Lever-action rifle
note: Lever under stock cycles bolt and chambers round. Allows fast fire from shoulder without bolt manipulation. Preferred for practical shooting because dominant hand never leaves grip.

name: Revolver
note: Rotating cylinder with six chambers. Simple mechanical operation, requires no magazine. Cylinder indexing requires precision tolerances. Sidearm of choice for cavalry and officers.

name: Self-loading pistol
note: Recoil or blowback operates slide to cycle bolt. Magazine holds 8-10 rounds. More complex than revolver but faster reloading. Becomes standard military sidearm after 1900.

name: Machine gun, recoil-operated
note: Recoil of firing cycle works the bolt. Bolt cycles faster than hand can move, enabling sustained fire. Requires cooling and ammunition supply. Changes tactics from cavalry to entrenchment.

name: Machine gun, gas-operated
note: Taps gas from barrel rear to drive piston. More controllable than recoil operation, runs cooler. Becomes preferred design for sustained fire roles because cooling load is lower.

name: Water jacket
note: Water-filled steel sleeve around barrel dissipates heat. Allows sustained fire for hours instead of minutes. Adds weight and complexity but multiplies practical sustained rate of fire.

name: Belt feed system
note: Cloth or steel belt carries linked rounds to feed mechanism. Eliminates magazine changes, extends firing duration. Enables crew-served weapons with sustained fire roles.

name: Smokeless powder
note: Nitrocellulose burns in stages, producing higher pressure without black powder's smoke. Higher velocity, longer range, less fouling in the bore. Shifts tactical range from 300 to 1000 yards.

name: Cordite
note: Nitrocellulose extruded into stick form with petroleum jelly as binder. Consistent burn rate, no dust, stores without separation. British standard ammunition propellant.

name: Artillery piece
note: Cannon cast in bronze or iron, requires sustained 1300 C furnace and careful cooling. Replaces trebuchets. Wall-battering capability becomes political.

name: Trunnion
note: Horizontal pins on barrel sides that rest in cradle to support gun at any angle. Enables elevation adjustment and absorption of recoil. Precursor to the carriage system.

name: Artillery carriage
note: Timber frame with wheels and trail spike. Cradle holds trunnions, allows elevation and traverse. Must be robust enough for road movement and firing stresses. Becomes larger with more powerful guns.

name: Recoil mechanism
note: The recoil mechanism is what lets a gun stay aimed between shots, which multiplies rate of fire far more than any improvement to the barrel. Hydraulic and spring system absorbs energy smoothly. French 75 mattered because it was the first truly quick-firing gun.

name: Breech block
note: Wedge or interrupted thread closes rear of barrel for breech-loading. Sliding or screw-in designs differ in speed vs seal. Requires precision tolerances to prevent gas leakage and chamber rupture.

name: Artillery shell
note: Hollow iron sphere filled with black powder and fitted with fuse. Bursts on impact. Different from solid shot, extends damage area beyond direct hit.

name: Shrapnel shell
note: Filled with lead balls and black powder, bursts in air by time fuse before ground impact. Sprays projectiles over area. Designed by Henry Shrapnel, becomes primary anti-personnel load.

name: High explosive shell
note: Bursts by impact detonator rather than burning fuse. Nitroglycerin or dynamite inside creates pressure wave that demolishes fortifications. Changes fortification design completely.

name: Artillery fuse designs
note: Time fuse burns at set rate to burst in air, percussion fuse detonates on impact, mechanical fuse uses spring striker. Fuse choice determines how shell fragments are distributed.

name: Mortar
note: Short barrel on fixed pivot fires at high angle over walls. Simplest gun, most robust, slowest. Chamber is conical. Low muzzle velocity means it does not need recoil control.

name: Howitzer
note: Intermediate angle gun between mortar and cannon. Longer range than mortar, higher angle than gun. Breech loading enables fast fire. Becomes dominant field artillery.

name: Indirect fire
note: Gun crew calculates aim without seeing target, firing over obstacles and terrain. Requires forward observer to report and adjust. Tripled effective range of artillery.

name: Forward observer
note: Soldier at front observes and communicates adjustments by telegraph or radio. Allows gunners to fire without line of sight. Feedback loop enables rapid correction.

name: Range table
note: Computed tables show elevation and powder charge for distance. Eliminates trial-and-error ranging. Based on ballistic equations. Single table distributed to hundreds of guns.

name: Rangefinder
note: Optical stereo matching measures distance to target. Baseline typically 1-2 meters. Accuracy within 100 meters at 10 km. Enables first-shot hits.

name: Fire control director
note: Central control station receives rangefinder and compass data, calculates firing solution for multiple guns. Synchronizes fire from battery. Naval ships use this to hit moving targets.

name: Fire control computing
note: Mechanical calculator using differential gears solves ballistic equations. Predicts future position of moving target, accounts for wind. Enables engagement of fast warships.

name: Anti-aircraft gun
note: Rapid-fire gun on rotating mount with high elevation angle. Feeds ammunition by belt. Requires predictor to aim ahead of aircraft. Effective only in large numbers.

name: Proximity fuse
note: Radio tube in shell detects reflected signal from aircraft, triggers detonation at closest approach. Creates lethal radius without direct impact. Transforms air defense effectiveness.

name: Trace italienne
note: The bastion answers the cannon because a round tower has dead ground at its foot where attackers hide, and an angled bastion does not. Low angled walls cannot be battered. Defense trades height for firepower.

name: Bastion
note: Angled stone structure jutting from wall allows cannon to fire along curtain, eliminating dead ground. Acute angle makes it harder to breach. Replaces round tower.

name: Glacis
note: Sloped ground in front of fortification. Denies attacker cover and lets defenders fire down. Attackers climbing upslope are exposed. Cheap to construct compared to stone walls.

name: Ravelin
note: Detached angled structure in front of curtain with its own garrison. Allows firing from front and sides, makes breaching the main wall harder. Additional layer of defense.

name: Casemate
note: Vaulted gunroom inside fortification, protected by stone and concrete. Guns fire through embrasures. Protects crew from enemy fire while operating guns. Becomes standard in 19th century.

name: Armoured cupola
note: Rotating steel dome houses gun and protects crew. Face-hardened armour resists artillery shells. Allows 360-degree fire. More expensive per gun than casemate.

name: Concrete fortification
note: Portland cement concrete resists artillery better than stone and is cheaper. Can be cast in place quickly. Allows reinforcement by iron bars or steel. Modern fortifications are mostly concrete.

name: Trench
note: Ditch protecting infantry from machine gun fire and artillery. Requires drainage and reinforcement with wood or concrete. Labor-intensive but fast to construct. Becomes primary infantry defense after 1900.

name: Barbed wire
note: Steel wire with sharp barbs, strung between posts. Cheap to produce and deploy. Impedes infantry advance and creates predictable fire zones. Dominant defensive obstacle.

name: Machine gun nest
note: Reinforced position for machine gun with interlocking fields of fire. Gun crew protected by concrete and guns. Key to trench defense. Can hold line with few troops.

name: Pillbox
note: Low concrete bunker with gun ports, designed to be nearly immune to artillery. Garrison of 4-6 can hold for hours. Difficult to assault frontally due to wide fields of fire.

name: Anti-tank ditch
note: Wide, deep ditch impassable to tanks. Steep sides prevent crossing. Requires sappers to bridge. Labor-intensive but effective when combined with mines and gun positions.

name: Plate armour against firearms
note: Plate armour against firearms and why it lost - musket balls penetrate at medium range, weight exceeds cavalry endurance, cavalry becomes less viable. By 1700, infantry with muskets dominates armoured cavalry.

name: Ironclad
note: Wooden hull with iron plate bolted to sides, steam-powered. Immune to cannon fire from other wooden ships. Requires dock infrastructure for repair. 1860 revolution in naval warfare.

name: Armoured cruiser
note: All-steel hull with partial belt armour. Fast enough to catch merchant ships, heavily armed. Cruises distant stations. Loses to battleship in combat but cheaper to build.

name: Dreadnought
note: The dreadnought and the all-big-gun idea - uniform main battery, all secondary guns removed. Higher speed than previous battleships, longer range artillery. Made all earlier battleships obsolete.

name: Battlecruiser
note: Battleship guns and armour but faster by sacrificing belt thickness. Intended to outrun battleships while catching cruisers. Vulnerable in battle when facing fully-armoured opponents.

name: Face-hardened armour
note: Hardened steel face with tough steel back. Impact on hardened face shatters projectile while backing absorbs energy. Lighter than solid plate for same protection.

name: Torpedo
note: Cylindrical vessel with explosive warhead, propelled by steam engine or compressed air. Destroys capital ships below waterline where armour is thin. Makes battleships vulnerable to small boats.

name: Torpedo boat
note: Small fast steam-powered boat carrying torpedoes. Fast approach under cover of night, fire and withdraw. Cheap compared to battleships, forces capital ships to operate in fleet formations.

name: Destroyer
note: Fast ship designed to hunt and destroy torpedo boats. Carries torpedoes itself and some artillery. Becomes primary fleet escort ship. Designed to counter the threat it was born from.

name: Submarine
note: Submerged vessel powered by battery or diesel engine. Surfaces to attack or recharge. Difficult to detect and counter. Single submarine can sink fleet carriers. Changes naval strategy fundamentally.

name: Periscope
note: Tube with prisms that allows viewing from below water surface. Enables targeting while submerged. Right-angle optics crucial for practical submarine attack.

name: Torpedo tube
note: Pressurized cylinder that launches torpedo using compressed air or water pressure. Must eject cleanly without tilting torpedo. Used in ships and submarines.

name: Depth charge
note: Explosive charge in steel canister, detonated by pressure fuse at set depth. Attacks submarines that cannot be reached by gun. Concussion in water is highly destructive.

name: ASDIC
note: Acoustic sonar using ultrasonic waves. Detects submarine by echoes. Requires trained operator to interpret. Revolutionary for anti-submarine warfare. Makes surface ships able to find and attack submerged vessels.

name: Naval mine
note: Buoyant sphere or cylinder containing explosive charge, triggered by contact or electrical current. Sinks ships silently. Danger persists after war ends. Forces careful navigation of coastal waters.

name: Minesweeper
note: Small vessel with dragging equipment or electromagnetic coil to detonate mines safely. Wooden hull to minimize magnetic signature. Essential for protecting shipping lanes and fleet movement.

name: Tank
note: Tracked armoured vehicle with gun turret, powered by petrol or diesel engine. Crosses trenches, immune to machine gun fire. Requires logistics supply line. Enables breakthrough tactics.

name: Track system
note: Linked metal plates forming endless belt around wheels. Distributes weight over large area, enabling crossing soft ground and obstacles. Reduces ground pressure compared to wheels.

name: Sponson
note: Gun mounting on side of tank hull, projecting outward. Provides wider firing arc than turret alone. Early tanks use multiple sponsons with different ammunition types.

name: Tank turret
note: Rotating armoured structure housing gun, rotates independent of hull. Allows aiming without turning vehicle. Requires internal ring and bearings. Becomes standard by 1920.

name: Turret traverse mechanism
note: Powered gear system rotates turret. Hand cranks for manual, hydraulic or electric for faster operation. Speed of turret traverse determines engagement capability.

name: Sloped armour
note: Angled armour plate increases effective thickness and deflects projectiles. Provides same protection with less weight than vertical plate. Requires improved cast or welding techniques.

name: Armoured car
note: Light armoured vehicle on wheels. Faster and lighter than tank, requires good roads. Carries machine gun and crew. Suited for reconnaissance and internal security.

name: Half-track vehicle
note: Wheels in front for steering, tracks in rear for power. Lighter than tank but terrain-capable. Carries troops or specialised equipment. Faster than tracked vehicle on roads.

name: Self-propelled gun
note: Artillery gun mounted on tracked chassis with armour. Mobile fire support that travels with infantry. Protects gun crew from machine gun fire. Becomes main fire support vehicle.

name: Observation balloon
note: Tethered balloon holding observer above battlefield. Sees enemy movement and artillery target locations. Vulnerable to artillery and aircraft. Telephone line to ground crew.

name: Aerial reconnaissance
note: Aircraft or balloon observing enemy positions, calculating range and bearing. Transmits by telephone or radio to artillery. Enables fire beyond line of sight.

name: Aerial camera
note: Fixed camera in aircraft or balloon taking photographs of landscape. Analysts study prints for enemy positions. Repeatable, accurate, less vulnerable than observers to small arms fire.

name: Bomb, general purpose
note: Streamlined iron casing with explosive charge and impact fuse. Falls from aircraft. Fragmentation pattern and crater size depend on casing thickness and bursting charge.

name: Bomb sight
note: Optical and mechanical system for calculating bomb release point. Accounts for altitude, airspeed, wind, and gravity. Mechanical computers solve ballistics equations. Dramatically improves accuracy.

name: Machine gun synchroniser
note: The machine gun synchroniser is why it is a genuinely clever piece of timing. Mechanical cams or hydraulic valve time gun fire to gaps in propeller blades. Allows firing through propeller without damage.

name: Fighter aircraft
note: Fast manoeuvrable aircraft with multiple guns. Engages enemy aircraft in combat. Requires skilled pilot training and logistics. Control of airspace determines ground tactical options.

name: Bomber aircraft
note: Larger aircraft carrying bomb load and defensive guns. Requires fighter escort against enemy fighters. Strategic bombing campaign against factories and cities. Needs radar and navigation aids.

name: Dive bomber
note: Aircraft that dives steeply to release bomb at low altitude for accuracy. High g-forces on pilot and aircraft structure. Accurate against small targets like ships. Effective against tactical targets.

name: Aircraft carrier
note: Warship with flight deck and aircraft. Replaces battleship as capital ship. Range and lethality determined by aircraft, not guns. Naval battles fought by planes beyond visual range.

name: Arrester wire
note: Steel cables across deck, aircraft hook catches wire to slow landing. Hydraulic or spring damping prevents jerking pilots. Enables landing on pitching flight deck in seconds.

name: Aircraft catapult
note: Steam-powered shuttle accelerates aircraft to flying speed in short distance. Allows heavier aircraft and full fuel loads. Enables launch with bomb and fuel load from moving ship.

name: Radar
note: Radiofrequency pulses detect aircraft at distance. Cathode ray tube display shows bearing and range. Enables detection through clouds and darkness. Changes air defence from visual tracking to radar guidance.

name: Chain Home radar network
note: The chain home idea - distributed radar stations reporting to central control centre which directs fighters. Early warning gives time to scramble interceptors. Won the Battle of Britain.

name: IFF system
note: Identification Friend or Foe - radar transponder in aircraft responds to interrogation. Allows ground radar to distinguish friendly from enemy aircraft. Eliminates tragic friendly fire incidents.

name: Guided bomb
note: Bomb with radio receiver and control surfaces. Radio operator in aircraft steers bomb to target. Dramatically increases accuracy. Operator must see bomb fall, limited by smoke and darkness.

name: Ballistic rocket
note: Liquid or solid fuel rocket follows ballistic trajectory. Reaches targets beyond artillery range. Difficult to intercept in flight. Changes strategic targeting doctrine.

name: Jet fighter aircraft
note: Gas turbine jet engine replaces piston and propeller. Much higher speed and altitude capability. Requires more fuel per hour but outpaces propeller-driven fighters completely.

name: Chlorine gas weapon
note: Chlorine and phosgene and mustard as weapons with an honest note on what they did - chlorine gas released upwind of trenches. Causes choking and lung damage. Casualties and demoralisation disproportionate to deaths. Introduced April 1915.

name: Phosgene gas
note: More toxic than chlorine. Causes pulmonary oedema, soldiers drown in fluid from their own lungs. More difficult to detect by smell, lulls victims into complacency. Called cocainised gas by soldiers.

name: Mustard gas
note: Blistering agent that damages skin and mucous membranes. Oily liquid, persists in soil and clothing. Casualties mount over days as soldiers do not realise exposure until burns appear. Deadliest chemical of the war.

name: Gas mask
note: Charcoal filter and glass eyepieces allow breathing filtered air. Early models inadequate against phosgene and mustard. Better filters developed by 1916. Makes chemical gas less decisive.

name: Flamethrower
note: Pressurised tank of burning petroleum with ignition system. Sprays flame 30-40 meters. Clears trenches and bunkers. Operator vulnerable during reload. Demoralising effect exceeds practical damage.

name: Incendiary bomb
note: Bomb filled with burning petroleum or white phosphorus. Ignites buildings and structures. Scattered from aircraft in quantity. Creates firestorms in wooden-built cities. Destroys civilian housing.

name: Napalm
note: Jellied petroleum that sticks to skin and burns. Developed late in World War 2. Continues burning after impact, causing severe burns. Area denial weapon that fills woods and buildings.

name: Atomic bomb
note: The atomic bomb as a single node with an honest statement: requires the isotope separation and reactor programme it needs and the fact that it is the one node in this tree whose use is a mass atrocity. Hiroshima and Nagasaki killed 150,000-200,000 civilians, mostly instantly. Nuclear weapons end conventional warfare through deterrence.

name: General staff
note: Permanent peacetime cadre of professional military planners. Plans campaign strategy, logistics, and mobilisation. Prussian innovation copied by all great powers.

name: War college
note: Educational institution teaching military science and strategy to officers. Studies history, tactics, logistics. Produces doctrine and fosters professional culture.

name: Logistics as discipline
note: Scientific study of supply, transportation, and distribution. Quantity calculations, transportation networks, storage facilities. Armies succeed or fail on logistics more than tactics.

name: Railway timetable mobilisation
note: The railway timetable as mobilisation instrument - detailed train schedules transport armies to frontier in days. Prussia mobilised in 14 days in 1866. Russian delays in 1914 cost the war. Coordination of five mobilisation timetables impossible without telegraph.

name: Field telephone
note: Telephone for battalion and company command. Connects front line to artillery. Enables real-time adjustment of fire. Requires cable laying and maintenance under fire.

name: Wireless set
note: Portable radio transmitter-receiver for unit command. Eliminates need for telephone cables. Message delay and security risk compared to telephone. Becomes standard by 1940.

name: Signals intelligence
note: Interception and analysis of enemy radio transmissions. Direction finding locates transmitter positions. Traffic analysis reveals unit movements and intentions without decrypting messages.

name: Cryptanalysis
note: Breaking enemy ciphers by systematic analysis. Enigma machine broken by Polish and British cryptanalysts. Ultra intelligence shortened war by years. Single intelligence source changes strategic decision-making.

name: Operational research
note: Scientific analysis of military operations to optimise doctrine and tactics. Statistical study of aircraft attrition rates, convoy losses, and radar effectiveness. Improves resource allocation.

name: Ammunition standardisation
note: Single cartridge specification across all rifles in army. Simplifies supply, enables ammunition interchange. Same powder, bullet, brass for all units. Doubles logistics efficiency.

name: Arsenal and interchangeable manufacture
note: The arsenal and interchangeable manufacture of small arms - Enfield rifles from Woolwich, Springfields from Springfield Armory, Mausers from Oberndorf. Jigs and fixtures ensure parts fit any rifle. Enables mass replacement of damaged weapons.

name: Conscription and reserve
note: Conscription and the reserve - compulsory military service produces trained reserve of millions. Mobilised in 1914, European armies grew from 2 million to 15 million within months. Trench warfare consumes manpower at unsustainable rates.
